newsitem.title: USA: Shell details Gulf Mexico spending, denies reports.
newsitem.headline: Shell details Gulf Mexico spending, denies reports.

text.p: Shell Oil Co, the U.S. subsidiary of the Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch/Shell Group, gave furter details Friday on proposed spending in the Gulf of Mexico and made clear that recent newspaper reports of planned $10 billion deepwater expenditure over the next four years were incorrect.

In a statement, the company said that it plans a total of $2.5 billion in exploration and production spending for 1997, out of a total $3.8 billion captial expenditure budget. The bulk of this will be in deepwater and other Gulf of Mexico projects.
"We continue to be focused specifically on Gulf of Mexico opportunities, both Shelf and deepwater," said Shell Oil spokeswoman Kitty Borah.

"We continue to have expenditures related to development of our announced discoveries. We have some additional discoveries (both Shelf and deepwater) for which we have funds allocated to do initial development but we prefer not to be any more specific on these discoveries at this time," she added.
Specifically, new 1997 spending will be focused on the Shelf project 'Enchilada', as well as development of deepwater fields Ursa, Mensa, Ram-Powell and Troika.

Shell has said that it has 12 other deepwater discoveries at various stages of evaluation, apart from the 10 announced, which include Augur, Mars, Tahoe, Southeast Tahoe, Popeye and Cardoman, as well as the four mentioned above.
However, Shell says that reports in two British newspapers on Thursday claiming that Shell Oil will spend $10 billion on deepwater Gulf projects over the next four years were untrue.
"I don't know how that figure was arrived at but it didn't come from Shell," said Borah. "We don't know what will be spent over that time but $10 billion is an inaccurate number...it is too high."
The number appears to have been derived by looking at the $2.2 billion spent to date, mainly on Augur and Mars, and extrapolating that amount based on projects in hand.

However, it didn't take into account the vastly variable costs involved in different types of projects and the fact that Shell is likely to take partners on a number of projects, thus spreading the costs. Nor did it factor in the experience Shell gained in its initial developments of the Mars and Augur fields.
